wari-bateshwar.desc: Two neighbouring villages in Belabo upazila sit on an ancient settlement that archaeologists date back to roughly the 5th century BCE. Excavations have uncovered a fortified enclosure with ramparts and a moat, a brick-paved road, punch-marked silver coins and semi-precious stone beads, suggesting links to wider trade networks. Much of the site looks like ordinary farmland, so a little imagination and a local guide help a lot. A small display and the excavated pits give a sense of what lies beneath.
blocks: How to get there
From Narsingdi town take a bus or CNG towards Belabo/Marjal, then a local auto to Wari village.
Good to know
Excavations usually happen in the dry season; visit in winter for the best chance of seeing work in progress.

glance: 41 km to Narsingdi by road, 1–2 hours by bus or car
Entry ticket plus separate charges for rides and the water park; check current prices
dream-holiday-park.desc: Dream Holiday Park at Panchdona, just outside Narsingdi town, is one of the best-known theme parks within easy reach of Dhaka. It has rides for children and adults, a water park, open lawns for picnics and a resort for those who want to stay the night. On Eid holidays and Fridays it fills with families and school groups. It is an easy day out rather than a heritage stop.
blocks: How to get there
Take any Dhaka–Sylhet or Dhaka–Narsingdi bus and get off at Panchdona; the park is beside the highway.
Good to know
Weekdays are far less crowded than Fridays and Eid. Carry a change of clothes if you plan to use the water park.

glance: Village homes and winter pitha fairs around Narsingdi, especially at Poush Sankranti
narsingdi-nakshi-pitha.desc: Nakshi pitha is made from a stiff rice-flour dough that women carve with date-palm thorns, bamboo slivers or moulds into flowers, leaves and geometric designs. The cakes are fried and then soaked in gur syrup, so they come out crisp outside and sweet within. Folk tradition credits the craft to village women of the Meghna side of Narsingdi, and the district is still the name most linked with it. It is made mostly for Poush Sankranti, weddings and winter gatherings, and given as a gift.

narsingdi-handloom.desc: Weaving has long been the backbone of Narsingdi's economy, especially around Madhabdi. Many families once worked handlooms at home, and today the clack of power looms fills village lanes alongside the older looms. Saris, lungis, gamchas and bedcovers made here are sold across the country. Walking through a weaving village gives you a sense of how much of Bangladesh's everyday cloth starts here.
blocks: Good to know
Ask before photographing inside homes and workshops.

narsingdi-sagar-kola.desc: Banana is Narsingdi's leading fruit crop, and the district is known for sweet, aromatic varieties such as sagar and amritasagar. Bunches are carried by van and boat to big wholesale haats before heading to Dhaka. Ripe ones are soft with a rich, slightly floral flavour. A hand of local bananas with tea and muri is a classic roadside snack.

glance: 41 km to Narsingdi by road, 1–2 hours by bus or car
baburhat-cloth-market.desc: Narsingdi's Madhabdi and Sheikherchar area grew rich on weaving, and the haat at Baburhat is its trading heart. On market days traders from across Bangladesh crowd its lanes buying saris, lungis, gamchas and grey cloth straight from local mills and looms. It is a working wholesale market rather than a tourist bazaar, which is its appeal. Come to watch the trade and pick up a gamcha or lungi at a fair price.
blocks: How to get there
Bus to Narsingdi on the Dhaka–Sylhet highway; Baburhat is beside the highway west of Narsingdi town.
Good to know
Go on a main market day; ask locally which days the haat is busiest.

bir-sreshtho-matiur-rahman-museum.desc: Flight Lieutenant Matiur Rahman, awarded Bangladesh's highest gallantry honour for his attempt to fly a jet out of Pakistan in 1971, came from Raipura in Narsingdi. A memorial museum and library was opened at his ancestral village, the former Ramnagar, on 31 March 2008, as part of a project to build such centres at the birthplaces of all seven Bir Sreshthos. It holds a library of a few thousand books and displays on his life, though none of his personal belongings. It is a short, meaningful stop for anyone travelling the Dhaka–Sylhet highway.
blocks: How to get there
From Narsingdi town or Bhairab, take a bus along the Dhaka–Sylhet highway toward Raipura and then a short auto ride to the museum.
Good to know
Check opening days locally; small rural museums often close on Fridays or public holidays.

glance: 41 km to Narsingdi by road, 1–2 hours by bus or car
narsingdi-meghna-riverside.desc: Narsingdi town lies close to the Meghna, one of the country's largest rivers. From the launch ghat you can hire a boat out towards the chars, low sandbanks where farmers grow vegetables in the dry season. At dusk the river turns gold and the silhouettes of bulk carriers and fishing boats slide by. It is an easy, low-key outing at the end of a day of sightseeing.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw from Narsingdi town to the river ghat.
Good to know
Agree the boat fare first; wear a life jacket if one is offered and avoid stormy afternoons.

narsingdi-lotkon.desc: Lotkon has a thin, leathery yellow skin that peels easily to reveal three or four juicy, slightly sour segments. Narsingdi supplies a large share of the country's crop, and in season lorries carry it to Dhaka. It is eaten fresh, often with a pinch of salt and chilli. It is cheap and makes a refreshing snack on a sticky day.

glance: 41 km to Narsingdi by road, 1–2 hours by bus or car
shibpur-lotkon-orchards.desc: Lotkon (Burmese grape) grows on the trunks and lower branches of its trees rather than on the tips, so a fruiting orchard looks as if it is wrapped in yellow beads. Shibpur and Belabo upazilas are the country's best-known lotkon areas, with orchards on red-soil land. Farmers are often happy to let visitors walk in during harvest. Buy a few kilos straight from the tree.
blocks: How to get there
From Narsingdi town take a CNG to Shibpur, then ask locally for lotkon orchards.
Good to know
Harvest runs roughly June–August. Ask permission before entering a private orchard.
